pedagogy.summary: Extending the standard columnar algorithm to whole numbers with more than four digits. The procedure is identical to four-digit work — align by place value, compose on carrying, decompose on borrowing — but scale raises the stakes: subtraction from large round numbers (500,000 - 234,178) forces an exchange that ripples across many zeros, and adding three or more five-digit numbers produces carries greater than one. Estimation-first and inverse checking remain essential because a single misaligned digit is now worth thousands.
bestPractices: Reinforce that nothing new is happening — same exchange rule, just more columns — to prevent 'big numbers are different' anxiety
Estimate by rounding before computing so a place-value slip in the thousands/ten-thousands is caught
Deliberately include a subtraction from a round number with several zeros (the extended borrow-across-zero)
When adding three or more numbers, make the >1 carry explicit ('13 ones = 3, carry 1 ten... but this column totals 24, carry 2')
Use place-value headers / squared paper so five- and six-digit numbers stay aligned
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns with headers to hundred-thousands
Base-ten / place-value counters for the exchange rationale
Empty number line for the estimate and for counting-up subtraction
commonMisconceptions: Extended borrow-across-zero fails — cannot cascade an exchange through several zeros (500,000 - 234,178)
Smaller-from-larger bug persists at larger scale
Misaligns digits when numbers have different lengths
When a column totals 20+ (three addends), carries only 1 instead of 2
Checks by redoing rather than estimating or using the inverse

learn.summary: Extend the standard columnar algorithm to whole numbers with more than four digits. The procedure is identical to four-digit work (align by place value, compose when carrying, decompose when borrowing), but larger scale raises the stakes: subtracting from a large round number such as 500,000 − 234,178 forces an exchange that cascades across several zeros, and adding three or more five-digit numbers can produce carries greater than one. Estimation-first and inverse checking matter more because a single misaligned digit is now worth thousands.

activities.title: Borrowing across a row of zeros (500,000 − 234,178)
feedback: If the child stalls at the zeros or does not carry the exchange through every column (e.g. 265,832, where the tens was left as 10 instead of 9, or 275,822, where the ten-thousands was left as 10 instead of 9), model with place-value counters: exchange one hundred-thousand and walk it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 with a ten passed on until the ones hold 10.
If a smaller digit is subtracted from a larger one regardless of position, do a concrete exchange on the failing column and reassert that you cannot take more than is there without borrowing.
If the child checks only by redoing the same subtraction, scaffold the estimate (round both numbers) and the inverse addition, or a counting-up number line, instead of reteaching the algorithm.
activities.rationale: Borrow-from-zero is a well-documented systematic subtraction bug that intensifies when a minuend has several adjacent zeros, so a deliberate round-number case targets the most-failed large-number hazard. A live place-value/counters model can animate the exchange as the child performs it; physical counters, squared paper, or a counting-up number line serve the same rationale without requiring a specific tool.
sourceClaims: Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug (Brown & Burton, 1325 students, 107 occurrences): the student changes a 0 to 9 but fails to continue borrowing leftward. When a minuend has several adjacent zeros (e.g. 500,000) the exchange must cascade through them, and this zero-borrow bug intensifies; smaller-from-larger (54 students) persists at scale. These are stable procedural bugs — ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour — not carelessness.
Composing/decomposing (exchange) is the conceptual basis of the columnar algorithm regardless of digit count; DfE Appendix 1 sets out the formal written methods.

Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
learnerActions: Set out 500,000 − 234,178 in columns aligned by place value, from the ones on the right.
Before computing, estimate by rounding (about 500,000 − 234,000 = 266,000) and note the expected size of the answer.

At the ones there is nothing to take 8 from, and every column to the left is 0; work the exchange by taking one hundred-thousand and walking it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 as a ten is passed along, until the ones finally hold 10.
Check with the inverse: 265,822 + 234,178 should return 500,000, and compare to your estimate (~266,000).
Optionally model the same subtraction as counting up on an empty number line — jump from 234,178 up to 500,000 and total the jumps — as an independent alternative that should also give 265,822.
Optionally repeat with an easier round-number case such as 500,000 − 234,000 and discuss why that borrow is simpler.
activities.intendedInsight: A single exchange can cascade through a row of zeros — each zero becomes a 9 as the ten is passed along, and the ones finally hold 10 — so a wall of zeros is not a dead end.

activities.title: Adding three numbers of up to five digits: when the carry is more than one
feedback: If the child carries only 1 from a column totalling 20 or more (e.g. 9 + 8 + 7 = 24), total the column aloud, separate it into 4 ones and 2 tens, and make the size of the carry explicit.

If a three-number sum is too small by exactly one (or more) in the column just above a heavy column (e.g. 10 too small when the ones totalled 24 but only 1 was carried), this may point to an undersized carry. Recount that column and check how many tens it holds.
If numbers of different lengths are misaligned so place values don't line up, use squared paper or place-value headers anchored from the ones on the right.
activities.rationale: A child drilled only on two-addend sums tends to assume a carry is always 1; a three-addend column that totals into the twenties surfaces and corrects that assumption. The original diagnostic problem does not actually create such a column, so a correctly chosen example is used for the larger carry while the given problem still serves alignment and repeated-carry practice. A part-whole bar can make the multi-addend structure explicit. A fill-in-the-blank format on carried digits plus a rounded estimate can assess this at scale but cannot verify handwritten alignment, so paper setup should also be observed.
sourceClaims: Composing/decomposing (exchange) is the conceptual basis of the columnar algorithm regardless of digit count; DfE Appendix 1 sets out the formal written methods.

Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
learnerActions: Set out 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 in a single column layout, aligning by place value from the ones on the right (numbers of different lengths must still line up); optionally show the three addends as parts of a part-whole bar whose whole is the total.
Add the ones column aloud and name the full total (0 + 6 + 8 = 14): write 4, carry 1.

Work through the rest of this sum: note that every carry here is only 1 (column totals including carries: tens 10, hundreds 11, thousands 16; the ten-thousands totals 3 with no carry), finishing at 36,104. This is good practice at keeping three different-length addends aligned and tracking repeated carries.

Now tackle a case that genuinely produces a larger carry, e.g. 36,489 + 27,858 + 15,937: the ones column totals 9 + 8 + 7 = 24, so write 4 and carry 2 (not 1); completing it gives 80,284, with several columns (ones, hundreds and thousands) carrying 2.
Compute 34,567 + 28,945 = 63,512 as a clean two-addend check that the basic algorithm is intact.
Estimate by rounding before computing so a place-value slip in the thousands or ten-thousands is caught.
activities.intendedInsight: When a column of three or more addends totals 20 or more, the carry can be 2 (or more), not automatically 1. (Not every three-addend sum reaches that — 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 only ever carries 1 — so a case whose column actually totals into the twenties is needed to surface the larger carry.)

activities.title: Worked-example reference and estimate-then-check routine
feedback: If the child's answer is far from the estimate, that gap is the signal to recheck alignment and exchanges (and quickly confirm the rounding in the estimate itself). Do not simply change the estimate to match the answer.
A revealed worked example is reference only; the child should then set out and solve a fresh case themselves on paper.
Praise specifically when the child catches their own error via estimate or inverse, reinforcing why that beats redoing the sum.
activities.rationale: Rounding-to-check is a statutory expectation and a reliable guard against single-digit place-value slips at scale; the inverse operation is independent of the original method, so it catches errors a re-run would reproduce. A revealed worked example is a useful static reference but exercises recognition rather than independent construction, so it must be paired with the child doing the work.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
learnerActions: Study a tap-to-reveal or step-by-step worked example of the across-many-zeros borrow, revealing each 0-becomes-9 exchange in turn to see the cascade clearly.
For every large calculation, first write a rounded estimate, then compute, then compare the answer to the estimate.
Check subtractions with the inverse addition (or a counting-up number line) and additions with an estimate rather than by redoing the same calculation.

Answer prompts: roughly how big should 500,000 − 234,178 be before working it out? Why did all those zeros turn into 9s? Would 500,000 − 234,000 be easier to borrow, and why? Why carry 2 and not 1 when a three-addend column totals into the twenties?
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating first and checking by the inverse catch place-value slips that are now worth thousands; redoing the same method just reproduces the same error.

constraints: This is a doing-on-paper procedural skill: the child must actually set out and compute the algorithm, not only recognise or describe correct steps.
Reinforce that nothing new is happening — same exchange rule, just more columns — to prevent 'big numbers are different' anxiety.

Deliberately include at least one subtraction from a round number with several zeros (the extended borrow-across-zero) and at least one three-or-more-addend sum whose column genuinely totals 20 or more (so a carry of 2 actually occurs).
Use place-value headers or squared paper so five- and six-digit numbers of different lengths stay aligned from the ones on the right.
A fill-in-the-blank or slider-based quiz can check carried/borrowed digits and estimates but cannot verify handwritten alignment, so observe paper setup directly.
A tap-to-reveal worked example is a static scaffold exercising recognition; it supports but does not replace independent construction on paper.

Base-ten counters, an empty number line, and on-screen place-value models offer different experiences of the exchange; any can make the cascade or the structure concrete, and none is strictly required.
Checking must use estimation or the inverse operation (or an independent counting-up method), not a re-run of the same calculation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

ORIGINAL ERROR CORRECTED: the row's assess.correctAnswer/diagnostic states the three-addend sum 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 'carries 2 where a column totals 20+', but no column of this sum reaches 20 even with incoming carries (column totals 14, 10, 11, 16, 3) — it carries only 1 throughout. To actually demonstrate a carry of 2, an agent-proposed example 36,489 + 27,858 + 15,937 = 80,284 is used (ones 9+8+7=24, write 4 carry 2; self-audit: 36,489+27,858=64,347, 64,347+15,937=80,284; columns carrying 2 are ones, hundreds and thousands). This replacement example is an unvalidated agent proposal and was not independently verified.

Representations restored: the original row's empty number line (estimate / counting-up subtraction) and part-whole bar (multi-addend structure) were only implicit in the earlier draft and are now offered as explicit optional representations.

The original catalog rationale claimed a conversation 'cannot exercise' a written algorithm and that a third dimension 'adds nothing'. These are fit judgements, not pedagogical laws; softened to narrow affordances/limits (dialogue supports but does not substitute for doing it on paper; the task is planar, so a 3D model offers no clear added value here).
One source (NRICH place-value material; DfE Appendix 1) is marked verified:false / not fetched this session; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: Roughly how big should the answer to 500,000 - 234,178 be, before you work it out?
Why did all those zeros turn into 9s when you subtracted?
What if it had been 500,000 - 234,000 - would the borrowing be any easier?
When you added the three numbers, why did you carry 2 and not 1 from the ones column?
assess.correctAnswer: 34,567 + 28,945 = 63,512 (composes through the columns). 500,000 - 234,178 = 265,822, cascading one exchange through the zeros. The three-addend sum = 36,104, carrying 2 where a column totals 20+. Estimate for the subtraction approx 500,000 - 234,000 = 266,000, close to 265,822; inverse 265,822 + 234,178 = 500,000.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot cascade an exchange through several zeros in 500,000 - 234,178 - stalls, or borrows only one column and leaves the rest as 0/9 wrongly
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model with place-value counters: exchange one hundred-thousand and walk it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 with a ten passed on.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Wrong middle digits (e.g. 265,882, 275,822) or the child freezes at the wall of zeros

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position (smaller-from-larger bug) at five-digit scale
errorPatterns.nextMove: Concrete exchange on the failing column; reassert you cannot take more than is there without borrowing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Columns 'flipped' wherever the top digit is smaller

errorPatterns.pattern: When the three-addend column totals 20 or more, carries only 1 instead of 2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Total the column aloud (13 + 8 + 6 = 24), separate into 4 ones and 2 tens; make the size of the carry explicit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The three-number sum is out by a multiple of ten in the next column up

errorPatterns.pattern: Misaligns digits when the numbers differ in length, so place values do not line up
errorPatterns.nextMove: Squared paper / place-value headers, anchored from the ones on the right.

errorPatterns.pattern: Checks by redoing the same subtraction rather than estimating or using the inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the estimate (round both) and the inverse addition; do not reteach the algorithm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The check reproduces the original method

responseLevels.gap: Misaligns, or breaks down at the row of zeros; carries only 1 from a 20+ column; no sense of the answer's size.
responseLevels.full: Solves all three including the zero-cascade subtraction and the double carry, aligns correctly, AND verifies with an estimate and the inverse; transfers to a similar round-number subtraction.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the clean addition and can describe the steps, but fails the across-many-zeros exchange or the >1 carry, or checks only by redoing and never estimates.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three to set out and solve on paper, watching alignment and exchange: 34,567 + 28,945; 500,000 - 234,178; and add these three in one column: 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058. Then ask them to check the subtraction by estimating and by the inverse.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 500,000 - 234,178 forces an exchange through five zeros - the extended borrow-across-zero, the most-failed large-number case. The three-addend column forces a carry greater than one, which a child drilled only on two-addend sums mishandles. The clean addition confirms the basic algorithm is intact, so failures localise to the scale-specific hazards.
